title: VIII. Communication and Language: The Social Channel

html:
The social-cognitive systems described in Sections I-VII all depend on a communication channel through which agents exchange information about internal states, intentions, norms, and world models. While non-human primates communicate through gestures, vocalizations, and facial displays, human language represents a qualitative expansion of channel capacity: a discrete combinatorial system capable of transmitting arbitrary propositional content–including content about absent entities, hypothetical scenarios, others’ mental states, and abstract norms–with a bandwidth and precision unmatched by any other biological signaling system. Language is not merely a tool used by a social mind; it is a co-evolved component of the social-cognitive architecture, and many of the systems described above (recursive mentalizing, norm transmission, reputation management, narrative identity, cultural learning) could not function at human scale without it.

Pragmatic Inference: Communication as Recursive Mentalizing

The computational core of linguistic communication is not grammar but pragmatic inference: recovering the speaker’s intended meaning from an utterance that underdetermines it. Grice’s cooperative principle 1–the expectation that speakers are informative, truthful, relevant, and clear–is a shared generative model of communicative behavior that enables listeners to infer intended meaning by reasoning about why the speaker chose this utterance rather than alternatives. This is explicitly a mentalizing computation: the listener must model the speaker’s beliefs, goals, and knowledge state to recover meaning. "Can you pass the salt?" is decoded as a request (not a question about ability) only by inferring the speaker’s communicative intention via the mentalizing system. Bayesian models of pragmatics formalize this as recursive social reasoning: the listener reasons about a speaker who reasons about a listener 2, engaging the same recursive modeling architecture described in Section I. The tight coupling between language comprehension and mentalizing is confirmed by neuroimaging: pragmatic inference recruits the mentalizing network (dmPFC, TPJ, temporal poles) over and above lexico-semantic processing 3, 4, and individuals with impaired mentalizing (e.g., autism spectrum) show corresponding pragmatic deficits even with intact syntax 5.

Language as a Reputation and Norm-Transmission Channel

Language dramatically amplifies the social systems described in previous sections:

Reputation via gossip: Language enables third-party reputation transmission–agents can learn about others’ past behavior without direct observation. Gossip (which likely constitutes the majority of spontaneous conversation 6) functions as a distributed reputation-tracking system: norm violations and cooperative acts can be broadcast through the social network, making reputation consequences extend far beyond the dyadic encounter. This massively increases the cost of defection (one act of cheating can be reported to the entire group) and the returns to prosociality (one act of generosity can enhance reputation network-wide) 6, 7.

Norm transmission: Explicit instruction, narrative, and moral discourse allow norms to be transmitted with propositional precision–specifying not just "don’t do XX" but the conditions, exceptions, justifications, and punishments associated with XX. This enables the culturally cumulative norm systems described in Section VII: each generation inherits not only behavioral norms but the rationale structure behind them, allowing selective modification rather than wholesale reinvention 8.

Narrative identity: Language enables the construction of a narrative self-model (Section III)–a temporally extended, causally structured account of "who I am and how I got here"–that goes far beyond the trait-level self-representation available to non-linguistic creatures. Narrative identity integrates episodic memories into a coherent life story that can be communicated to others, evaluated against cultural templates (redemption arcs, contamination sequences 9), and used to coordinate mutual expectations in relationships.

Neural Implementation

The dual-stream language architecture and its social interfaces. The perisylvian language network–left IFG (Broca’s area) for hierarchical structure building and articulatory planning, left posterior STG/STS (Wernicke’s area) for phonological and lexico-semantic processing, connected via arcuate fasciculus and other dorsal/ventral pathways 10, 11–provides the syntactic-semantic processing engine. But crucially, this engine is densely interconnected with the social-cognitive networks described throughout this paper:

Anterior temporal lobes / temporal poles: The convergence zone for semantic person-knowledge, social concepts, and narrative comprehension–providing the interface between linguistic representations and the person-model database (Section I) 12.

Mentalizing network (dmPFC, TPJ): Recruited during pragmatic inference, irony/sarcasm comprehension, indirect speech acts, and narrative perspective-taking–all cases where recovering meaning requires modeling the speaker’s mental states 3.

STS voice-selective regions: Analogous to face-selective areas, voice-selective cortex along bilateral STS provides a dedicated processing channel for paralinguistic social cues–vocal identity, emotional prosody, speaker confidence, and deception markers 13–that are processed in parallel with and inform the interpretation of linguistic content.

Evolutionary and developmental trajectory. Language acquisition follows a genetically timed sensitive period with well-characterized milestones (babbling ∼\sim6 months, first words ∼\sim12 months, grammar explosion ∼\sim18-36 months 14) and depends on both domain-specific architectural priors (lateralized perisylvian cortex, vocal tract anatomy, statistical learning biases) and obligate social input (contingent interaction with speakers; language cannot be acquired from passive exposure alone 15). The social gating of language learning–infants learn phonemes from live social interaction but not from equivalent audio/video exposure 15–demonstrates that the language faculty is architecturally embedded within the social-cognitive system: the learning mechanism itself requires the ostensive communicative cues (eye contact, contingent turn-taking, joint attention) that signal "this is addressed to you" and that depend on the social-attention and mentalizing circuits described in Section I. Language is not a general-purpose computational tool that happens to be used socially; it is a fundamentally social technology whose acquisition, processing, and deployment are gated by social-cognitive architecture at every level.
